title: MB9-25181
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX XXXX (the appellant), a citizen of Mexico, is appealing against the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting his claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX (the appellant), a citizen of Mexico, is appealing against the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting his claim for refugee protection.
The appellant stated that he fears three men who threatened to kill him if he reported their assault against an individual in the street.

The RPD found that the appellant was not credible because his behaviour was not that of a person who is fearful. While his testimony was trustworthy, it rejected his claim because it was of the opinion that he faces a generalized risk.

The appellant argued that the RPD erred in finding that he lacked credibility based simply on his motives for not moving and on the fact that these motives were not reasonable. The RPD also erred in referring to the risk as generalized when the appellant had been specifically targeted by his assailants because he had witnessed their crime.
The Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) is of the opinion that the determinative issue is the internal flight alternative (IFA).
The RAD confirms the RPD's determination and dismisses the appeal.

After the appellant witnessed three men assaulting an individual on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017, these men allegedly assaulted and threatened to kill the appellant if he reported them. In the weeks and months that followed, these men allegedly pursued, harassed, insulted and threatened to beat the appellant on several occasions. He reportedly changed jobs to avoid them. He allegedly opened a XXXXshop in another neighbourhood in the city. The men reportedly found him, continued to mistreat him, and took his earnings and merchandise. The appellant then supposedly decided to leave the country.
On XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018, he allegedly left Mexico for Canada, where he claimed refugee protection. His wife and son reportedly remained in Mexico.
The RAD conducted an independent analysis of all of the evidence, including listening to the recording of the hearing before the RPD, and it applied the correctness standard.1

After listening to the recording of the hearing, the RAD notes that the RPD questioned the appellant about the possibility of relocating to the cities of Mérida or Campeche in Mexico. However, the RPD did not mention this in its reasons. Seeking to raise this matter in its reasons, the RAD asked the appellant, in accordance with the principles of procedural fairness and natural justice, to provide submissions on the possibility of him relocating to the cities of Mérida and Campeche. The appellant sent his submissions to the RAD within the specified timeframe.

The RAD will not address the arguments the appellant raises in his memorandum regarding the generalized risk, since it is of the opinion that the appellant does not face a prospective risk in the IFA. For the same reason, it will not address the appellant's credibility unless required in the context of the IFA analysis. Internal flight alternative

In Rasaratnam2 and Thirunavukkarasu,3 the Federal Court of Appeal defines the test to be applied when assessing an IFA. There are two prongs to the test: 1. The Board must be satisfied on a balance of probabilities that there is no serious possibility of the claimant being persecuted or, on a balance of probabilities, that he would not be subjected personally to a risk of harm in the part of the country to which it finds an internal flight alternative exists.4 2. Conditions in the part of the country considered to be an IFA must be such that it would not be unreasonable, in all the circumstances, including those particular to the claimant, for him to seek refuge there.5
Both prongs must be satisfied to find that an IFA exists. First prong

The onus was on the appellant to establish that in the IFA proposed by the RPD in the cities of Mérida and Campeche, he would face a serious possibility of persecution under section 96 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), or that he would, under subsection 97(1) of the IRPA, on a balance of probabilities, be personally subjected to a risk to his life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment. The RAD is of the opinion that the appellant did not do so.

The RAD did not conduct an analysis under section 96 of the IRPA since the evidence does not establish a nexus to one of the five Convention grounds, namely race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group and political opinion. The analysis must be conducted pursuant to subsection 97(1) of the IRPA, specifically paragraph 97(1)(b) of the IRPA.

In his submissions,6 the appellant claims that he has established that the agents of persecution have the ability and willingness to find him. His written and oral testimony demonstrate that the three men are motivated to pursue him in the suggested IFA in Campeche or Mérida. After the incident of XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017, the men allegedly tracked him down at his work and harassed him. Then in mid-XXXX, he reportedly opened a XXXX shop in a different neighbourhood from where he used to work, and in less than a month, the men found him. According to the appellant, if the men were to discover that he was back in Mexico, they would look for him again because he is able to identify them. The appellant cited the following excerpt from the National Documentation Package (NDP) on Mexico:7 "...a large debt or a personal vendetta could motivate a gang to track someone outside their area, and that gangs can use 'corrupt law enforcement agents' to obtain information about people they pursue."
The RAD is of the opinion that the evidence does not establish the three men's ability to track the appellant in the suggested IFA.

After listening to the recording of the hearing before the RPD, the RAD notes that when the appellant was asked what means these men had to find him in the suggested IFA, he responded8 that they could have ties to armed gangs, more dangerous criminal gangs that could be linked to drug traffickers that are sometimes in collusion with police officers and operate with complete impunity. The RPD asked what made him believe that they would have ties to organized crime, and the appellant explained9 that there is tremendous insecurity in Mexico and that these are large-scale criminals who will not think twice before eliminating someone. The appellant then acknowledged10 that he did not have any evidence that these three men were linked to organized crime, but that he fears for his life.

The RAD is of the opinion that the three men's potential involvement in organized crime or drug trafficking is speculative. Furthermore, the appellant acknowledged that he has no evidence of such an affiliation, and the RAD saw nothing in the facts to support this affiliation.

The RAD also failed to accept the appellant's argument that, because the men allegedly found him after he had left his job and started a business in another neighbourhood in the same city where he lived, they would supposedly be able to find him in another region of Mexico.

The appellant testified11 that he did not believe the men knew where he lived. He stated that when they were following him as he was getting off the bus, he tried to take different routes home, and when he was headed away from residential neighbourhoods, he waited in areas with bushes to see if people were following him. If the three men did not manage to follow the appellant and find his home, which is located closer to his store than his previous job,12 the RAD is of the opinion that the evidence does not establish, on a balance of probabilities, that they would find him in another city.
Contrary to the appellant, the RAD is of the view that the evidence does not establish that the three men would be able to find him in the cities of Campeche or Mérida.

Since it was concluded that the appellant did not demonstrate that the three men would be able to find him in the suggested IFA, examining their motivation is not technically required. Nevertheless, the RAD chose to proceed with the analysis.

According to the RAD, the NDP on Mexico mentioned earlier and to which the appellant referred13 to support this argument that the men are motivated to find him, does not apply to these circumstances. It is a response to a request for information on drug cartels, their activities, areas of operation and ability to track individuals within Mexico. The excerpt cited by the appellant is in the section on the ability of cartels to track people. The RAD is of the opinion that the appellant did not establish that the three men belonged to a drug cartel. Therefore, this documentary evidence does not support the appellant's statement that the three men are motivated to track him down.

The appellant argued in his submissions that the three men allegedly have an interest in finding him since he is able to identify them. After listening to the recording of the hearing, the RAD notes that the appellant testified14 that the three men would have an interest since they did not want to leave any trace of or witness to the attack.

The RAD does not accept this argument. It is of the view that the three men would have had every opportunity to eliminate the appellant if they had wanted to since, according to his written account and his testimony, they tracked him down at his work and then at his store on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017. For the rest of XXXX 2017 and in XXXX 2018, when the men were intoxicated, they would regularly steal his merchandise and his earnings; they insulted him and threatened to make him disappear.15

The appellant notes in his memorandum, in the context of the analysis of the second prong, evidence that he believes demonstrates that he would not be safe in Mérida or Campeche due to the prevalence of crime. The RAD is of the opinion that the evidence does not demonstrate this, as will be outlined later. It also does not support the claim that the appellant faces a personal risk.

The RAD is of the opinion that the appellant did not demonstrate, on a balance of probabilities, that he would be personally subjected to a risk of harm in the cities of Mérida and Campeche. Second prong

The Federal Court of Appeal set a very high threshold for what makes an IFA unreasonable: "It requires nothing less than the existence of conditions which would jeopardize the life and safety of a claimant in travelling or temporarily relocating to a safe area. In addition, it requires actual and concrete evidence of such conditions."16

In his submissions, the appellant claims that it would be unreasonable for him to relocate to Campeche or Mérida with his wife and son. He would supposedly have a hard time settling there, and finding employment and housing. He would not be able to rely on his family members since they have all died, except for two sisters who live in the city where he resides, and who are therefore of no help. He has only nine years of education and few options are available to him given that he has always lived in the same city.

In response to the RPD's opinion that the fact that he did not move-because he did not know where to go-was unreasonable, the appellant argues in his memorandum17 that moving to another state with a wife and son calls for significant planning since it is a life change that requires starting from scratch and finding suitable housing, which is an enormous burden. Moreover, the three pay stubs he produced demonstrated his low salary, and with a son to provide for, he could not afford to leave his work and move without reflecting on it for a while and without having had time to save some money.

The appellant also states in his submissions that the documentary evidence demonstrates that he would not be safe in Mérida or Campeche. To support his statement, he cites a source from the NDP on Mexico which focuses primarily on crime and safety in the states of Quintana Roo, Yucatán, and Campeche:18 Generally, Mexican police must concentrate their limited resources on urban areas. For Quintana Roo, Yucatán, and Campeche, police presence and emergency response are extremely limited outside of the state capitals, population centers, and tourist areas. State Police dedicate some resources to rural areas where there may be little or no municipal rule of law, but response times are usually high, and police prioritize cases of active threats or violent crime. Levels of professionalism vary greatly among police agencies. Consequently, citizens are often indifferent to police authority.

The RAD is of the opinion that the appellant did not submit any actual or concrete evidence on the conditions in Mérida and Campeche that would jeopardize his life and safety. He did not demonstrate that it would be unreasonable for him to live there.

After listening to the recording of the hearing before the RPD, the RAD notes that, in the context of its questions about the IFA, the RPD inquired as to whether it was possible for the appellant to find employment in another city. The appellant acknowledged19 that the job he had prior to opening his XXXXshop was a common occupation in Mexico, but he stated that he did not know if he could find a similar job in another city. He testified20 that when he ran his shop, he had enough income to cover the household needs and purchase products to sell. Moreover, in response to a question from his counsel about whether he could find employment if he returned to Mexico, the appellant stated21 that he could probably find one, but he would not feel safe.

The RAD notes that in one of the forms the appellant completed upon arriving in Canada,22 he listed all of his occupations from 2008 to 2018. He reported that he was unemployed from 2008 to 2010, and that he had fairly steady employment from 2010 until his arrival in Canada in XXXX 2018. He was a XXXX XXXXaXXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXthen a XXXXand finally a XXXX.

The RAD understands that leaving a city where one has lived their entire life can be challenging and comes with its share of difficulties, especially with limited resources and education, and without anyone's help to settle in the new location chosen. That said, the appellant has had various occupations throughout the years. He has not established that he would not be able to find employment in the cities of Mérida or Campeche. The appellant also had some success with his shop since, after opening it in XXXX 2017,23 he had enough income to support his family until his departure from Mexico in XXXX 2018.

The RAD notes that the documentary evidence the appellant referred to on security and crime in the states of Campeche, Yucatán and Quintana Roo is aimed at American travellers. It provides an assessment of the threat of crime against US government interests, and the introduction makes reference to the security level in the states of Campeche and Yucatán:24 This is an annual report produced in conjunction with the Regional Security Office at the U.S. Consulate in Mérida. OSAC encourages travelers to use this report to gain baseline knowledge of security conditions in the three Mexican states on the Yucatán Peninsula: Campeche, Yucatán, and Quintana Roo, which include the tourist destinations of Cancún, Cozumel, Isla Mujeres, Playa del Carmen, Tulum, and the coastal area referred to as the Riviera Maya. ... The U.S. Department of State has assessed Mérida as being a MEDIUM-threat location for crime directed at or affecting official U.S. government interests. According to Government of Mexico statistics, Yucatán and Campeche are among the safest states in Mexico.

Consequently, this document reports that according to the Government of Mexico, the states of Campeche and Yucatán are among the safest states in Mexico. The RAD is of the view that it does not support the appellant's statement that he would not be safe in Mérida or Campeche. The excerpt cited by the appellant does not support it either since it states that police and emergency services are concentrated in the capitals, urban centres and tourist areas. Mérida and Campeche are both the capitals of their states and urban centres,25 and would therefore receive these types of services.
The RAD concludes that it has not been established that it would be unreasonable for the appellant to live in Mérida or Campeche.
The RAD is of the opinion that the appellant has an IFA in the cities of Mérida and Campeche in Mexico.
The RAD concludes that the RPD's decision is correct, but for different reasons.

The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the RPD's determination that the appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
